newsitem.title: UAE: FEATURE - UAE's vast oil wealth misses poor villages.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UAE's vast oil wealth misses poor villages.

text.p: The elderly man with one tooth sat near his goats in this mountain hamlet and pondered 25 years of independence in the United Arab Emirates.
"How can we celebrate?" asked Mohammad Rajeel, 80. "We have no electricity so there is no television to watch celebrations. There is no car to go to town either."

The vast petrodollar fortune which transformed the Gulf's impoverished desert sheikhdoms into a global oil power never blessed Wadi al-Fayy and some other villages in the UAE federation's poor emirates.

There will be no firecrackers or traditional bedouin dancing below the jagged, mud-coloured mountains that surround Wadi al-Fayy, home to 15 families who sleep on straw mats in concrete shacks with wooden or sheet-metal roofs.

Rajeel said he and other farmers would spend their time praying on December 2, when the UAE celebrates a quarter century of immense oil wealth that has financed a cradle-to-grave welfare state, five-star hotels and fleets of limousines.
The period has been dominated by rapid development in the richest emirates, Abu Dhabi and Dubai, where modern skyscrapers tower over broad boulevards.

Abu Dhabi owns vast oil reserves that give its nationals one of the world's highest per capita incomes estimated at $29,000 a year. Dubai, the commercial heart of the UAE, is a regional trade and re-export centre with a booming economy.
The other members of the federation are Sharjah, Ras al-Khaimah, Umm al-Qaiwain, Ajman and Fujairah.
Abu Dhabi contributes most of the federal money to the poorer emirates that lack significant sources of income.
They are just a few hours' drive away but worlds apart from Wadi al-Fayy, on the Gulf of Oman about 200 km (125 miles) northeast of Dubai.
Poles for electricity lines have been transported to the village recently. They are mostly lying on the ground but residents hope for power supply in the next few months.
There is no running water -- people walk the dirt track that winds through the mountains to reach wells.
School buses that climb the track are the only sign of modernity.

While foreign labourers dominate a wide variety of manual jobs in Abu Dhabi and Dubai -- from building highways to trimming the lush shrubbery that lines them -- Wadi al-Fayy cannot afford the luxury of expatriate workers.
Every morning, 15-year-old Mohammed Saeed wakes up at five, walks up the steep mountains and spends the next five hours searching for bee hives.
"We try to find the hives so we can get honey to sell in town," said Mohammed, offering a bowl of dates and oranges to a visitor. "And then we spend our day working the fields."
Mohammed, his seven brothers and sisters and 75-year-old father Abdullah toil the fields to earn 300 dirhams ($81) a month by selling honey, vegetables and goats.
The government also gives them 1,800 dirhams a month, but they say it is not enough to cope with the price of staple foods in the market in Dibba, the nearest town.
"We want electricity and telephones. We just want the essentials and we will be happy," said Abdullah, sitting below a hunting rifle hanging on a wall.

Some residents of villages like Wadi al-Fayy have moved over the last few years to low-cost state housing units at the foot of the mountains. And some of the younger generation have migrated to cities in search of work.
"It's difficult to sustain life in the mountain farm settlements," said Marycke Jongbloed, head of the Sharjah Natural History Museum.
"The (new) villages are close to the main highway. Children go to school and they learn about the cities and they don't want to go back."
But the older villagers say they would not trade the simple life in the mountains for the glitter of the cities of plenty.
"We don't know oil. We don't know that kind of life," said one village elder.
"I was born here," he said, motioning to the mountains. "How can we leave? This is our life."
